story.title: Iceland Votes on Resuming EU Membership Negotiations in Referendum
story.summary: Icelanders are voting in a referendum on whether to resume negotiations for European Union membership. The decision comes after a decade-long suspension of talks, which were halted in 2013 following a shift to a eurosceptic government. The outcome of this referendum is being closely monitored, given its potential implications for Iceland's future relationship with the EU.

explore_lenses.label: What would a “yes” vote actually change?
explore_lenses.title: It reopens a paused accession process, not EU membership
explore_lenses.summary: The ballot asks whether Iceland should resume accession negotiations, not whether it should join the EU. Iceland's earlier application remains available for revival even though talks stopped in 2013 and Iceland said in 2015 that it was not seeking membership.

claims.text: The referendum question is whether Iceland should continue accession negotiations with the EU; it is not a vote to ratify EU membership.
Iceland applied in 2009, held negotiations from 2010 to 2013, and had opened 27 of 35 negotiating chapters, provisionally closing 11 before the process was put on hold.
The Icelandic government says the EU Commission has confirmed that Iceland's application was not formally withdrawn, so negotiations could be resumed if Iceland chooses.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: A positive result creates a political mandate to pursue talks, but does not itself secure an EU offer or any negotiated exemptions.

explore_lenses.label: Why are fishing and sovereignty central?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute is over control as much as trade
explore_lenses.summary: Supporters and opponents both frame the decision around sovereignty, but reach opposite conclusions: supporters say greater participation in European decision-making would strengthen Iceland, while critics focus on domestic control of lawmaking and fisheries.

claims.text: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir argues that EU membership can strengthen, rather than diminish, sovereignty for a small state; the government says Iceland currently lacks a seat when EU decisions affecting its interests are made.
Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of the eurosceptic group Heimssýn, argues that Icelandic independence depends on retaining the ability to make its own laws and decisions.

Fisheries Iceland CEO Heiðrun Lind Marteinsdóttir says her industry group would not oppose membership with a permanent fisheries-policy opt-out, but describes such an outcome as unprecedented and cautions that negotiators must be realistic.
Iceland's stated negotiating priorities include control over fisheries, sustainable use of marine resources, shared stocks and representation in international fisheries agreements.

explore_lenses.label: What would happen after the referendum?
explore_lenses.title: A long, multi-stage process would still follow
explore_lenses.summary: The referendum is advisory and is only the opening decision in a potential accession path. A “yes” would lead Iceland to ask the EU to restart the process; any final membership treaty would require further political and public approval.

claims.text: The National Electoral Commission says the referendum result is advisory under Iceland's Elections Act.
If voters favor talks, the government says it would convey that wish to the EU, and resumption would need formal confirmation at an intergovernmental conference between Iceland and EU member states.

Past chapter outcomes and Iceland's negotiating positions would need review and updating before negotiations proceed; after a complete deal, Iceland would hold a second referendum on the accession treaty.

Forecast: the process would take years, because it would involve negotiations across 35 policy areas and approval of any deal by all EU member states, according to AP's account of the accession framework.

story_report.summary: Icelanders are voting on whether to resume negotiations on joining the European Union, reviving an accession process suspended in 2013. The ballot is advisory and is not a vote to ratify membership, but a vote in favor would give the government a political mandate to tell the EU that Iceland wishes to return to talks. Any eventual accession agreement would require a separate referendum in Iceland.

sections.heading: Iceland’s Earlier EU Negotiations
sections.body: Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 and negotiated from 2010 until 2013. Before the process was put on hold, 27 of 35 negotiating chapters had been opened and 11 provisionally closed. The Icelandic government says the European Commission has confirmed that the application was never formally withdrawn, leaving a route to resume the process if the country chooses.

sections.heading: Sovereignty and Fisheries Divide Debate
sections.body: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir argues that membership could strengthen a small state’s sovereignty, saying Iceland lacks a seat when EU decisions affecting its interests are made. Eurosceptic campaigner Haraldur Ólafsson says independence depends on retaining control over Icelandic laws and decisions. Fisheries are central: Iceland’s priorities include control of the sector and marine resources, while the industry says a permanent opt-out would be necessary but unprecedented.

sections.heading: EU Accession Process After Vote
sections.body: If voters support renewed talks, Iceland would need to convey that decision to the EU, with resumption requiring formal confirmation at an intergovernmental conference involving Iceland and EU member states. Earlier chapter results and Iceland’s positions would then be reviewed and updated. The process is expected to take years, spanning 35 policy areas and requiring approval of any final agreement by every EU member state before Iceland’s later treaty referendum.

unresolved.text: A favorable referendum would not guarantee that the EU offers terms acceptable to Iceland, including any fisheries protections; no such arrangement has been agreed.
The duration and final terms of negotiations, required Icelandic constitutional steps, and the outcome of any later referendum on an accession treaty remain unknown.

related_stories.summary: President Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America.' In response to the order, Ontario Premier Doug Ford plans to unveil a new sign for Lake Ontario in Winona, Ontario.
